newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia trumpets anti-bribe moves amid doubts.
newsitem.headline: Russia trumpets anti-bribe moves amid doubts.

text.p: Russia's leadership has made an aggressive public start to its latest anti-corruption campaign, but is recycling some ideas that have already failed before, officials said on Sunday.

"The president has finally realised that this scourge must be fought," Nikolai Makarov, public prosecutor in Saratov region, south of Moscow, told Reuters. "Now, a more or less common front is being formed."
President Boris Yeltsin last week signed a decree and made a speech promising new moves against the corruption that has flourished across Russia since the fall of communism in 1991.
Then, in a rare Saturday session before television cameras, Russia's new First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov grilled government officials on the way they award state contracts.
Many officials, long accustomed to working behind closed doors, stumbled and were visibly uncomfortable.
"Why are your prices 50 percent higher than in regular stores?" Nemtsov demanded of an official overseeing a chain of stores providing goods to the military.
"Uh, we have a problem," the official meekly responded, looking up towards Nemtsov on a podium above and facing an auditorium of officials below.
"We don't have this problem -- there is a problem with the organisation of your work," Nemtsov said sharply.
Unlike a noisy anti-corruption campaign in 1992-93 that targeted high-level politicians, Yeltsin appears to be attempting to strike at the roots by opening state contracts to competitive bidding.
But critics say the latest moves are too little, too late.
"The (presidential) decree is not on the fight against corruption, but only on state purchases," said Yuri Boldyrev, Russia's prime corruption fighter until 1993.

"This of course is needed. But to get results we cannot just speak abstractly, we must set simple norms -- for example, a car for government workers cannot be purchased for more than $9,000," he told Reuters.
"But alas, there are no such norms."

Nemtsov, speaking on Russian public television on Saturday night, said the key to fighting corruption was "glasnost", or openness. He said if the government widely published upcoming purchase needs, and the bids received, then bribery would be much more difficult.
He added the president's office was working on new regulations requiring bureaucrats to declare their incomes and personal wealth as well as that of their families.
Boldyrev, now deputy director of Russia's general accounting office, said similar moves had already failed in the past.

"Five years ago the president issued a decree on fighting corruption, with a direct order to the government to introduce a system of income delarations for bureaucrats," he said. "For five years, the government itself has blocked this, and the president didn't demand the fulfilment of his decree."
"If Nemtsov really wants to do this, there are going to be great difficulties," he said.
Makarov, who as Russia's deputy public prosecutor in 1993 investigated charges against several Yeltsin allies, also warned that politicians should not meddle in corruption investigations.

"Back then it was a battle of compromising materials," he said in a telephone interview. "It would be a mistake to just concentrate on high officials; the struggle should be against the (corrupt) organs themselves."
